title: Augmenting Coaching with GenAI: Insights into Use, Effectiveness, and Future Potential
extended_summary:
This paper examines how professional coaches are currently using generative AI tools and what shapes their adoption, with particular attention to perceived benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and expectations for future use. The study is motivated by the rapid spread of large language models in professional workflows and by the lack of empirical evidence on real-world GenAI use in coaching. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, the paper asks how coaches already using GenAI integrate it into their practice and how they evaluate its usefulness and risks.

The study used an online survey of 205 active coaching professionals recruited through Prolific in January 2025. Participants were mostly health and fitness, business, career, and life coaches based in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other European countries. They reported on their use of text-based GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude across coaching tasks including research, content creation, administrative work, analysis, and relational support. The survey also measured AI literacy, positive and negative attitudes toward AI, ethical considerations such as transparency and privacy, perceived effectiveness, and expectations for future AI use.

Findings show that GenAI is already widely adopted for efficiency-oriented tasks, especially research, brainstorming, content generation, and administration, but is used less for relational and interpretive work. Higher AI literacy, positive AI attitudes, and stronger perceived impact of AI were associated with greater use. By contrast, negative attitudes, concerns about replacement, and ethical concerns did not significantly reduce current use. Frequent users reported greater awareness of ethical issues, especially transparency and privacy, and many respondents emphasized the need for stronger safeguards and coaching-specific tools. The paper concludes that GenAI functions mainly as an augmentation tool in coaching rather than a substitute for human coaches, while calling for better AI literacy training, ethical guidelines, and longitudinal research on how use evolves over time.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot / assistant for text generation, analysis, and conversational support.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of the text-based GenAI tools used by coaching professionals in their coaching practice; the paper reports ChatGPT 4.0 as the most frequently preferred primary tool.

findings.finding_summary: Among 205 coaching professionals, ChatGPT 4.0 was the most frequently preferred tool (65.4%). Nearly half of participants (49.8%) had used their preferred tool for more than one year, and 36.1% used it daily with another 36.1% using it multiple times per day. Coaches reported high perceived usefulness for research, automation, and content generation, while use was more limited for deeply interpersonal and interpretive tasks.
findings.measure: Self-reported tool preference, duration of use, frequency of use, and perceived effectiveness/role in coaching tasks

findings.finding_summary: In a multiple regression predicting GenAI use, perceived current AI impact, AI literacy, and positive AI attitudes were significant positive predictors, but negative AI attitudes, ethical considerations, expected future AI use, belief in AI as a substitute, and concerns about AI replacing coaching were not significant. The overall model explained 50.6% of the variance in GenAI use (R2=0.506, Adjusted R2=0.488, F(8,196)=25.343, p<.001).

The paper identifies privacy and confidentiality as a key ethical concern in coaches' use of ChatGPT-based tools, noting that almost 94% of respondents reported using a version of ChatGPT as their primary GenAI tool and that these tools are not set up for secure handling of personal, sensitive data. This is presented as an ethical limitation rather than an outcome effect.
findings.measure: Self-reported ethical considerations and discussion of data security/privacy risks

quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with self-report measures from coaches already using GenAI, so it provides useful descriptive and associative evidence but not causal or field-experimental evidence. The study is methodologically clear, but it is not a direct K–12 teacher coaching intervention study.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are substantial in size for adoption behavior (e.g., R2=0.506), but they describe use, attitudes, and ethics rather than learning or instructional outcomes. The paper suggests meaningful operational impact for coaching workflows, yet it does not demonstrate educational harm or benefit in K–12 teacher coaching specifically.
